status: Both A27 rulings are implemented and PROVEN end to end on a two-process core against local fixture origins. A 120-second drip-feed import that the shipped code kills at 60 s now imports and publishes; a hung origin and an over-budget transfer fail with two DIFFERENT typed reasons, each naming its knob in the worker log; a channel sync whose source is down is retried at 1x, 2x, 4x and then the cap instead of at the plain interval forever, survives a worker restart mid-backoff, is bypassed by sync-now, and resets on the first success. No register row changes: INT-02 stays PASS.
scope: Ruling 1 (per-read idle timeout + configurable total budget on URL import) and ruling 2 (exponential backoff on channel-sync failures), both recorded as limits in the A27 section.
frontend_revision: vidra-user import/hardening @ b67be96 + the strict-mode fix
search_revision: vidra-search NOT touched and NOT run

pull_requests.dependency_order: core#189 first (it carries the additive OpenAPI change and migration 0135), then user#182 (its contract-ci lane is red until core merges), then this meta PR.

migration: 0135_channel_syncs_failure_count — ALTER TABLE channel_syncs ADD COLUMN failure_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, with a matching .down.sql. Additive with a default, so existing rows read 0 (= no consecutive failures yet) and a deploy needs no backfill. core CI's prev-release-against-new-schema lane passes.

ruling_1_download_budgets.what_shipped: internal/urlsafety gains NewBudgetClient(Budget{Total, Idle}) beside the existing NewClient(timeout). Same SSRF policy — the identical net.Dialer.Control hook, nil Proxy, per-redirect ValidateURL, chain capped at 5 — with download-shaped timeouts instead of one whole-request deadline.

idle_timeout.why_that_default: it is the exact 60 s that used to bound the WHOLE request, now doing the job it was always good at: silence for a minute is a dead source on any link, while the transfer TAKING a minute says nothing about its health.
idle_timeout.mechanism: enforced on the CONNECTION — the returned net.Conn is wrapped so SetReadDeadline is reset before every Read. Because it sits under the transport it also covers the TLS handshake and the wait for response headers, not just the body.
idle_timeout.zero_means: the built-in default, NOT 'no idle bound'. Deliberately not symmetric with the total budget: an operator may sensibly want no total cap; nobody wants a download with neither bound. A negative value is refused at boot.
idle_timeout.typed_as: urlsafety.ErrIdleTimeout (an error that also satisfies net.Error Timeout(), so http.Transport's retry logic is unchanged, and errors.Is matches os.ErrDeadlineExceeded)

total_budget.why_that_default: it bounds how long one import may hold a worker slot; it does not police speed. UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE defaults to 2G, and 2 GiB in 6 h is about 0.8 Mbit/s — slower than any link an operator would import over, so the budget only fires on a transfer that is pathological rather than merely slow.
total_budget.mechanism: a per-request context deadline installed by a RoundTripper, carried through the response body and released on Close. http.Client.Timeout was deliberately NOT reused: its expiry surfaces as an untyped error a caller cannot tell from its own cancellation, so no failure message could name which limit fired.
total_budget.zero_means: no total cap (the house 0-disables convention, cf. YTDLP_MAX_HEIGHT=0)
total_budget.per_hop_caveat: the budget is applied per redirect hop, so a chain could in principle spend up to maxRedirects (5) times it. The meaningful case — the final large download — gets exactly one budget.

error_surfaces.job_error_idle: the download stopped receiving data from the source
error_surfaces.job_error_budget: the download took longer than this instance allows
error_surfaces.why_two_sentences: one says the source went quiet (nothing the operator configured is at fault); the other says this instance's own limit ended it.
error_surfaces.worker_log_idle: video import download stalled  job=… video=… limit=IMPORT_FETCH_IDLE_TIMEOUT idle_timeout=20s
error_surfaces.worker_log_budget: video import download exceeded its time budget  job=… video=… limit=IMPORT_FETCH_TIMEOUT budget=30s
error_surfaces.url_never_echoed: the direct resolver returns the BARE sentinel, never http.Client's own *url.Error, which carries the attacker-controlled URL. urlsafety's budget classifier drops the raw error for the same reason.

callers_of_guard_NewClient_enumerated.internal/videoimport/service.go: CHANGED — the download path now uses NewBudgetClient(Total, Idle). Its HEAD probe gets a separate short client: a probe transfers no body, so the idle timeout IS its whole-request budget; giving it the download's 6 h would let one unanswered HEAD stall a worker for hours before any bytes were in play.
callers_of_guard_NewClient_enumerated.internal/channelsync: makes NO guard.NewClient call at all. It lists through ytdlp.Client.Playlist (a --flat-playlist subprocess) and the media download is the videoimport ytdlp resolver, also a subprocess. So the channel-sync download path is bounded by YTDLP_TIMEOUT, not by these knobs.
callers_of_guard_NewClient_enumerated.internal/federation (follow.go, ingest.g: UNCHANGED — small ActivityPub JSON fetches/deliveries. A whole-request deadline is the CORRECT shape here: the response is small, so a response that takes longer than the deadline IS a failure.
callers_of_guard_NewClient_enumerated.internal/atproto (oauth_client.go x2, xr: UNCHANGED — same reason: short RPC-style calls.
callers_of_guard_NewClient_enumerated.internal/linkpreview: UNCHANGED — a bounded HTML head fetch, same reason.
callers_of_guard_NewClient_enumerated.internal/peertubeimport/lazystatic.go: UNCHANGED and stated deliberately — it IS a download path, but of images capped at 8 MiB, run by an operator's own migration tool against their own source instance, with a 20 s whole-request timeout. Left alone to keep this diff surgical; recorded as the one download caller that still uses whole-request semantics.

ruling_1_download_budgets.ytdlp_wall_clock: YTDLP_TIMEOUT (15m) STAYS as it is. yt-dlp is a child process, so there is no read to instrument — an idle timeout is not expressible there, and --max-filesize is what bounds its bytes. The consequence is worth an operator's attention and is recorded as a gap, not fixed: a very large PLATFORM download over a thin link still dies at 15 minutes, and raising YTDLP_TIMEOUT is the only lever.
ruling_1_download_budgets.runtime_overlay: Neither knob is an instance-settings row: both are env-only, like YTDLP_TIMEOUT next door. Changing one needs a restart.

ruling_1_measurements.measurement_caveat: each refusal above was measured on its FIRST attempt under the configuration named. import_jobs is a durable retrying queue and the worker was restarted between phases with different limits, so the end-of-run table shows some of those same jobs later succeeding (e.g. the size-cap drafts, once the cap was back at its default) or dead-lettering for a different reason (the stall job reached 5 attempts as 'could not fetch the URL' after its origin was stopped). The first-attempt evidence is what is cited.

ruling_2_channel_sync_backoff.what_shipped: consecutive failures are counted on the row (migration 0135) and the next attempt is CHANNEL_SYNC_INTERVAL * 2^(n-1), capped at CHANNEL_SYNC_BACKOFF_MAX. Reset to 0 by FinishChannelSync (the first success). Reuses internal/retry.Backoff, the same doubling every other queue here uses, with the sync cadence as its base.

knob.validated: must be a positive duration when CHANNEL_SYNC_ENABLED=true

sql_shape.ClaimDueChannelSyncs: RETURNING now includes failure_count, so a claim re-reads the PERSISTED counter
sql_shape.FailChannelSync: failure_count = channel_syncs.failure_count + 1 in SQL, so a stale Go-side read can never clobber it
sql_shape.TriggerChannelSyncNow: unchanged — next_run_at = now() is exactly the bypass; failure_count is deliberately left alone, so a manual run that also fails continues the widening rather than resetting it

ruling_2_channel_sync_backoff.api: GET/POST /channel-syncs now return failure_count (int32, required) and next_run_at (date-time, required) on ChannelSync. Additive to the schema; no route change.
ruling_2_channel_sync_backoff.lab_configuration: CHANNEL_SYNC_INTERVAL=1m, CHANNEL_SYNC_BACKOFF_MAX=6m, CHANNEL_SYNC_COOLDOWN=0s. The worker's channel-sync poll tick is a fixed 1 minute with jitter, so a run fires within about a minute of its due time; the SCHEDULING decision is exact and is read straight off the row.

creator_surface_in_real_chromium.how: the vidra-user production build served as node .next/standalone/server.js behind a pipe-only proxy on ONE origin (vidra_refresh is SameSite=Lax, Path=/api/v1/auth), driven by headless Chromium at 1440x1000, signed in as the creator, Studio → Channel.
creator_surface_in_real_chromium.failing_row_first_walk: http://localtest.me:8198/dead-feed.xml | Never synced · into Lab Channel | FAILED | could not list the external channel | 3 failed runs in a row · next attempt due now | Sync now | Remove
creator_surface_in_real_chromium.failing_row_second_walk: … | FAILED | could not list the external channel | 4 failed runs in a row · next attempt in 6m | Sync now | Remove  (the row's own next_run_at was exactly 360 s out)
creator_surface_in_real_chromium.healthy_row: http://localtest.me:8199/feed.xml | Last synced 1m ago · into Lab Channel | IDLE | Sync now | Remove — no failure line at all
creator_surface_in_real_chromium.rules: the line is suppressed for a healthy sync and while a run is in progress (during 'syncing', next_run_at is the worker's 30-minute lease expiry, not a scheduled attempt — rendering it would be a lie). A missing or unparseable next_run_at degrades to the count alone rather than 'in NaN'.
creator_surface_in_real_chromium.countdown_rounds_not_floors: a scheduled moment is always read some time AFTER it was scheduled, so flooring would render every backoff one unit short and a 4h gap would never once say '4h'.

for_a35_correlation_qoe_retention: Both new failure paths are stamped like every other import failure: the job_runs row carries request_id, correlation_id, actor_id, worker_id and the retry_scheduled state (verified on the stall job — claimed_at 13:11:08, updated_at 13:11:28). The two new worker log lines carry a structured `limit` field naming the env var that fired (IMPORT_FETCH_IDLE_TIMEOUT / IMPORT_FETCH_TIMEOUT), which is a cheap dashboard facet: 'imports ending on OUR limit' vs 'imports ending on THEIR silence' are different operational stories. channel_syncs is still NOT projected into job_runs — its only trace is the row plus the 'channel sync pass failed' warning, which now also carries consecutive_failures and retry_in.
for_a38_upgrade_rollback: Migration 0135 is additive with a DEFAULT, and core CI's prev-release-against-new-schema lane passes, so the previous release runs against schema 135 unchanged — it simply never reads or writes failure_count, which means a rolled-back binary reschedules failing syncs at the plain interval again while the counter sits frozen on the row. The .down.sql drops only the counter; next_run_at keeps whatever the last run scheduled, so an older binary resumes its plain cadence from there. Both new env keys are optional with in-code defaults, so an operator who upgrades without touching env/*.env gets the fixed behaviour (60 s idle / 6 h total) with no config change — that is the intended upgrade story and should be stated in the release notes, because the OLD behaviour (imports dying at 60 s) disappears silently.
